Add opt-in TFLOPs and MFU logging with LoRA aware FLOP counts (#13885)

This adds an opt-in callback that logs achieved TFLOPs per GPU and model
FLOPs utilization during training. Set `UNSLOTH_LOG_MFU=1` before
creating the trainer, or call
`unsloth.utils.mfu.add_mfu_callback(trainer)`. Training logs then gain
`train_tflops_per_gpu` and, when the GPU is known, `train_mfu`. With the
variable unset nothing changes.

The usual 6N per token estimate is wrong for LoRA. The FLOP count here
walks the linear layers: every layer pays 2n for the forward and 2n for
the input gradient, only trainable weights pay 2n for the weight
gradient, and gradient checkpointing adds one more forward for the
decoder layers (not the output head). Full finetuning comes out at 6N,
LoRA at about 4N plus the adapters. Attention adds 4 x layers x heads x
head_dim FLOPs per causal query key pair, three times for forward plus
backward and four times with checkpointing. Tokens and per sequence
lengths come from the batch (attention mask, packed sequence lengths or
padding free position ids), so padding is not counted.

The peak comes from a small table of dense 16 bit numbers (T4, L4, A100,
H100 variants, H200, B200, MI300X/A, MI325X) and can be overridden with
`UNSLOTH_PEAK_TFLOPS`, for example with a measured maximum achievable
matmul number. Unknown GPUs and fp32 training log TFLOPs only.

The callback is inserted first in the callback list so WandB,
TensorBoard and the progress bar see the new fields. Token counting
stays on device and syncs once per logging window.

Tests: `tests/test_mfu_logging.py` checks the counts against hand counts
on a tiny Llama for full finetuning, frozen weights, LoRA, and gradient
checkpointing, the attention term, sequence length extraction, the peak
table, and an end to end CPU Trainer run. On an L4 with Qwen2.5-0.5B
LoRA r=16 in fp16 the logged MFU settles around 12 to 15 percent.

Known limits: sliding window attention, MoE experts stored as 3D
tensors, vision towers and embedding lookups are not modeled, so those
models report an approximation.

Token budget: weight split-chunk TRL metrics by token count (#13978)

## Summary
With `UNSLOTH_TOKEN_BUDGET` set, a micro-batch over the budget runs
`training_step` once per chunk. TRL's SFTTrainer appends one
`mean_token_accuracy` and one `entropy` entry per `compute_loss` call,
then logs the plain mean of those entries. Unequal chunks were therefore
weighted equally. In one example the logged accuracy was 0.5, while the
same unsplit batch logged 0.25. Loss and gradients were already exact.

This change folds the per-chunk entries back into one entry per
micro-batch, weighted by the token count TRL divides by:
- accuracy: shifted labels that are not -100 (TRL 0.22.2 and 1.x)
- entropy: the label mask on fused-head TRL 1.x, and the attention mask
(plus prompt-tuning virtual tokens) or every position when padding-free
on TRL 0.22.2
- DDP: one all_reduce of the counts, only on split steps, matching TRL's
gather

## Scope
- Only the split branch changes. When the budget is unset, a step is not
split, or the trainer has no `_metrics`, the code path is the same as
before.
- Unsloth's generated SFT trainer does not append these metrics, so the
default Unsloth SFT path is unaffected. The fix covers unrewritten TRL
trainers (for example `UNSLOTH_ALLOW_CPU=1`, compile fallback) and
subclasses that log TRL-style metrics.

## Tests
- `tests/test_token_budget_metrics.py`: unequal chunks against TRL
0.22.2-style and 1.x-style metric code. 2 fail before this change and
all 4 pass after.
- Existing token budget, formatter and encoding tests: 100 passed, 2
skipped.

was 0.5), equal to the unsplit step. Entropy also matches.

Cover explicit RoPE position ids and compute the starting cache on CPU (#13976)

Follow-up to #13855.

**1. Explicit position ids past the lazily built cache**

`LlamaModel_fast_forward` now builds `max(seq_length_with_past,
max_seq_length)` rows of the cos/sin cache, but
explicit `position_ids` (offsets, generate prefill, packing) can index
any row below
`max_position_embeddings`, and the RoPE kernel gathers without a bounds
check. A tiny Llama with 131072 positions,
`max_seq_length = 2048` and `position_ids` starting at 40000 returns NaN
logits on main; with this change the
logits match the transformers reference.

When `position_ids` is passed, the model forward builds
`max_position_embeddings` rows again, as before #13855,
still only on the device that reads them, so the multi-GPU saving stays.
Bounding the positions exactly would need
a host sync per forward, so it is not done. Without `position_ids` the
short cache is kept.

**2. Starting cache computed on CPU again**

Before #13855 `__init__` computed the starting cache on CPU. Built
lazily, it was computed wherever loading had
moved `inv_freq` (CUDA on transformers 4.57.6), which raised the first
forward's peak memory (about 16 MiB to
64 MiB for 32768 rows at head dim 128) and changed cos/sin rounding.
`_set_cos_sin_cache` now computes on CPU
until the cache first grows, and on `inv_freq`'s device afterwards,
matching the old behaviour in both cases.

**Tests**

`tests/test_rope_cache_current_device.py` gains three tests: explicit
offset positions through the real model
forward block, the short cache without `position_ids`, and the starting
cache computed on CPU. Two fail on main
and all pass here; the existing RoPE, formatter and encoding tests pass
(72 passed, 2 skipped).

head_dim 512 attention: sm80+ only, no 256 MB autotune buffer, OOM falls back to SDPA, no per-call mask sync (#13977)

Follow-up to #13869 for three problems on the default-on path.

**T4 step time.** On a Colab T4, fp16 Gemma-4 E2B vision SFT (12 steps,
ABBA) ran 1.8% to 3.5% slower per step with #13869 than with its parent
or with `UNSLOTH_HD512_ATTENTION=0`. Yet the kernel never ran there: its
self check fails on sm75, and fp16 Gemma-4 text attention reaches SDPA
directly through the float32 path. The kernel was only timed faster on
sm80+. Pre-Ampere GPUs now skip the self check entirely (no compile, no
autotune), and the router is not installed when every device and dtype
of the model failed its self check. On the same T4 job, this change is
level with the kernel switched off (4300 / 4307 ms against 4403 / 4379
ms), with identical peak memory.

**Autotune memory.** Triton's default autotune benchmarker allocates a
256 MB L2 flush buffer. With head_dim 512 this happens in the load-time
self check, and again on the first forward and first backward of every
new GQA group size, because the autotune key is `(HEAD_DIM, G)` and the
self check only covers G = 2. A model that fit on the previous SDPA path
could therefore OOM at load or on its first training step. Under a 128
MB process cap, SDPA succeeds on a G = 8 call, while the kernel failed
allocating 256 MB. The self check also added 258 MB of peak allocation.

- The three autotuned kernels now time configs in place with CUDA events
(warmup, estimate, about 10 ms of reps) and allocate nothing extra.
Every config only rewrites its own outputs, so rerunning is safe. This
is set as the autotuner's `do_bench` attribute, which works on Triton
3.2 (where `autotune()` does not forward `do_bench=`) through 3.7.
`OutOfResources` handling for configs that do not fit is unchanged.
- An OOM in the self check now disables the kernel for that device and
dtype (SDPA, as before) instead of failing the load. An OOM in the
forward kernel falls back to SDPA for that call.
- Self check peak: 270,408,704 to 8,917,504 bytes. The G = 8 call under
the 128 MB cap now runs forward and backward on the kernel.

**Mask scan sync.** The router scanned the mask (one host sync) before
looking at the self-check verdict, and inference-mode masks, which
cannot cache the verdict, were rescanned on every layer. Left-padded
generation prefill is then rejected anyway. Masks are now scanned only
when the result can be used: not for inference-mode masks (they go
straight to the previous SDPA, unchanged) and not after a failed self
check. Training masks keep the one-scan-per-step cache.

**Tests:** 7 new tests in `tests/test_large_head_attention.py`:
benchmarker installed, self-check OOM, fresh autotune adds under 32 MB,
router OOM fallback, no scan for inference masks or after a failed
check, no compile before sm80, and no install when every self check
fails. The first 5 fail on the current main. Router and self-check GPU
tests now need sm80+. The full file plus the formatter and encoding
tests give 79 passed, 2 skipped.

**Not covered:** a Triton 3.2 run (checked against its source only),
sm80+ step time, AMD (the route stays off on ROCm), and a speed
comparison of the configs picked by in-place timing versus flush-based
timing.

Add `unsloth doctor --gpus` multi-GPU preflight and UNSLOTH_DEBUG_DISTRIBUTED (#13884)

Multi-GPU problems on consumer and cloud boxes usually show up as a hang
at the first collective, or as silently wrong peer copies on hosts with
a translating IOMMU. Today the only tool is
`scripts/p2p_integrity_probe.py`, which is aimed at llama.cpp and is not
part of the installed package. This adds a preflight that answers "will
distributed training work on this machine" before a long job starts.

`unsloth doctor --gpus` (also `python -m unsloth_cli doctor`) prints:

- torch, CUDA or ROCm build, driver and NCCL versions, and every visible
GPU with its compute capability, memory and PCI id
- the NVML topology per GPU pair (PIX / PXB / PHB / NODE / SYS, NVLink,
P2P read) when nvidia-ml-py is installed, matched to torch indices by
PCI bus id so CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES does not scramble it
- a peer copy integrity check for every ordered pair, using a
sentinel-filled destination
- an all_reduce across all visible GPUs in separate processes with a
short collective timeout and a hard deadline, so a hang is reported
instead of hanging the doctor, plus the measured bus bandwidth
- a verdict with hints. If the all_reduce fails or hangs it is retried
with NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1, and the hint says whether that fixed it. Peer
copy corruption points to NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 and the IOMMU log. PHB /
NODE / SYS links without NVLink recommend DDP for LoRA, since it only
moves the adapter gradients, over FSDP / ZeRO-3 / tensor parallel.

The exit status is 1 when a problem is found, so it can gate a launch
script.

Output on a Kaggle T4x2 (torch 2.14.1, NCCL 2.30.7):

```
=== Topology (NVML) ===
0<->1  PHB   nvlink=no  p2p_read=no

=== Peer copy integrity ===
0->1  peer_access=yes  ok
1->0  peer_access=yes  ok

=== all_reduce smoke (2 ranks, nccl) ===
ok  busbw 3.94 GB/s (64 MiB fp32)

=== Verdict: OK ===
- GPU pairs [(0, 1)] talk through the PCIe host bridge or the CPU interconnect (PHB / NODE / SYS), with no NVLink. For LoRA prefer DDP: it only all-reduces the small adapter gradients, while FSDP / ZeRO-3 and tensor parallel move the full weights every step over this link.
```

`UNSLOTH_DEBUG_DISTRIBUTED=1` is a single switch for hang debugging. At
`import unsloth`, before any process group exists, it sets
TORCH_NCCL_DESYNC_DEBUG=1, TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT=1, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO
and a 2000 entry flight recorder under the name the installed torch
reads: TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE on torch 2.8+, TORCH_NCCL_TRACE_BUFFER_SIZE
on 2.6 and 2.7 (2.7 defaults the recorder to off). Setting both would
make newer torch warn on every rank. Anything the user already set is
left alone, and the two buffer names are treated as one setting so an
explicit TORCH_NCCL_TRACE_BUFFER_SIZE=0 is respected. Without the flag
nothing changes.

Tests (CPU): `unsloth_cli/tests/test_doctor_gpus.py` runs a real 2-rank
gloo all_reduce, a forced hang, every verdict branch, the NVML pair
mapping with a fake pynvml and the full command with a faked 2-GPU
torch. `tests/test_debug_distributed_env.py` covers the env switch and
checks the hook runs before torch is imported.

FSDP2: save_pretrained, merged saves and 4-bit checkpoints for sharded models (#13895)

Stacked on #13880 (FSDP2 QLoRA), which is stacked on #13865 (FSDP2
core).

Under FSDP2 every parameter is a DTensor shard, so the save paths that
read module weights directly break:

- `model.save_pretrained()` fails in peft/safetensors ("invalid python
storage") for LoRA, QLoRA and full finetuning.
- `model.save_pretrained_merged(..., "merged_16bit")` fails inside the
zoo merge ("Cannot set version_counter for inference tensor").
- QLoRA `trainer.save_model()` and every Trainer checkpoint fail with
`'DTensor' object has no attribute 'absmax'`:
torch.distributed.checkpoint resolves bitsandbytes' `weight.absmax` keys
as attributes of the sharded weight. Training with `save_steps` dies at
the first checkpoint.

Changes:

- `unsloth/models/fsdp2_save.py`: `fsdp2_gathered(model)` reshards every
unit, all-gathers one parameter at a time, and on rank 0 swaps the full
tensors (CPU) into the modules for the duration of the save, then
restores the shards and barriers. 4-bit weights are gathered as raw
bytes and rebuilt as `Params4bit` with their QuantState, so a
dequantizing merge still works. Adapter saves gather only the trainable
weights.
- `save_pretrained` and `save_pretrained_merged` use it when the model
is FSDP2-sharded and no `state_dict` was passed: every rank calls the
save, rank 0 writes. Models that are not sharded are untouched.
- Inside torch's state dict helpers, bitsandbytes `Linear4bit` reports
only weight and bias, which fixes QLoRA checkpoints,
`trainer.save_model` and resume.
- Trainable parameters left out of FSDP2 (`ignored_modules`) now have
their gradients averaged across ranks; before, each rank stepped on its
own gradient and the copies drifted apart.

Evidence (2 GPUs, tiny Llama, bf16):

- Saved adapters and full weights are bit-identical to the gathered
trained parameters for LoRA, LoRA with trained embeddings and lm_head,
QLoRA and full finetuning.
- Merged checkpoints reloaded in plain transformers match the adapter
reload (max logit difference 2e-6 for LoRA and QLoRA) and equal the fp32
merge of the trained weights to 7e-9.
- Resume from a mid-run checkpoint reproduces the continuous run bit for
bit (losses, grad norms, learning rate, final weights) for LoRA, LoRA
with dropout, QLoRA and full finetuning. Zeroing the LoRA B weights or
the Adam moments in the checkpoint changes the resumed losses, so the
state really is loaded.
- New CPU test `tests/test_fsdp2_save_gloo.py` (2 gloo ranks) covers the
gather, the 4-bit byte round trip, the drift of ignored trainable
parameters and the checkpoint state dict of a sharded 4-bit model.

Merged saves hold the full model in rank 0 host RAM (like accelerate's
full state save), and save_pretrained must be called on every rank; a

FSDP2: shard QLoRA 4-bit weights with fused LoRA kernels kept on (#13880)

Stacked on #13865 (FSDP2 core); review that one first.

QLoRA under FSDP2 currently leaves every 4-bit weight replicated on each
GPU: bitsandbytes stores the packed bytes as uint8, which accelerate
excludes from sharding. This change shards them.

- When FSDP2 is requested, Unsloth quantizes with
`bnb_4bit_quant_storage` set to the compute dtype (float16 on T4,
bfloat16 elsewhere). Pre-quantized uint8 checkpoints are reinterpreted
in place as the same dtype (a view of the same bytes, no copy, same
QuantState).
- FSDP2 rebuilds the gathered weight as a plain Parameter and drops
`quant_state`. FSDPParam is wrapped so the sharded and the gathered
weight keep it, and the fused LoRA kernels fall back to the Linear4bit's
own QuantState if it is still missing.
- Mixed precision never casts packed 4-bit bytes.
- An all-gather holding packed weights always copies bytes. When all
inputs of a unit share one float dtype, FSDP2 copies them with
`torch._foreach_copy_`, which on CUDA rewrites float16 and bfloat16 NaN
bit patterns to the canonical NaN. About 1.7% of packed float16 words
were changed this way, which corrupted every 4-bit weight once LoRA was
gathered in the storage dtype.
- The FSDPParam and collective hooks are method wrappers, checked
against torch 2.6 to 2.14. If an anchor is missing, nothing is patched
and the weights stay uint8 (replicated, as before). The same happens
with accelerate older than 1.13, whose FSDP2 wrap upcasts the whole
model.

Results on 2 GPUs with a 2-rank FSDP2 run against the 1-GPU run at the
same per-forward batch, fused LoRA kernels on:
- tinyllama-bnb-4bit (2 x B200): the 4-bit weights per GPU go from 484
MB to 242 MB, and peak training memory from 1.56 GB (replicated) to 1.25
GB.
- Through the Trainer, the loss stays within 7e-4 of the 1-GPU run over
6 steps and the LoRA update cosine is 0.9999.
- The manual fully_shard run matches a 2-rank replicated run bit for
bit.
- On Kaggle T4x2 (fp16, torch 2.14), the Trainer FSDP2 QLoRA run stays
within 5e-4 of the 1-GPU loss with LoRA update cosine 0.99997, and the
packed weights per GPU are halved.
- On Kaggle T4x2 (fp16, torch 2.14) with tinyllama-bnb-4bit through the
Trainer: loss within 7.1e-4 of the 1-GPU run, LoRA update cosine
0.99989, 4-bit weights per GPU 484 MB to 242 MB and peak training memory
1.33 GB to 1.16 GB per GPU. On torch 2.9.1 a 100M model through the
Trainer stays within 1.4e-4 (cosine 1.0000).

Tests: `tests/test_fsdp2_qlora.py` (CPU, gloo, real bitsandbytes layers)
and `tests/python/test_get_lora_parameters_fsdp2_quant_state.py`.

The all-gather corruption also affects accelerate's documented bf16
FSDP2 QLoRA recipe (all-bf16 units), so it may be worth reporting
upstream separately.

Not covered: torch 2.6 to 2.8 keep uint8 storage (those versions require
one dtype per unit including frozen weights), so 4-bit weights stay
replicated there, as today; torch 2.10 to 2.12 were checked against
source only; accelerate older than 1.13 and transformers 4.57 are unit
tested only; gradient checkpointing under FSDP2 QLoRA, vision models and
8-bit were not run.

Studio: hide safetensors models that exceed VRAM when the fit filter is on (#13945)

## Problem

With "Only show models that fit" on, the Hub page keeps safetensors
models that their own row badge marks as over budget. On a host with 72
GiB of VRAM and 94 GiB of RAM, Safetensors format selected:

| Model | Row badge | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct | Likely fits · ~14.7 GB | listed | listed |
| Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct | Tight fit · ~66.8 GB | listed | listed |
| c4ai-command-r-plus-08-2024 | Over VRAM budget · ~94.8 GB | listed |
hidden |
| Mistral-Large-Instruct-2411 | Over VRAM budget · ~111.7 GB | listed |
hidden |
| falcon-180B | Over VRAM budget · ~163 GB | listed | hidden |
| Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct | Over VRAM budget · ~366.7 GB | hidden |
hidden |

## Cause

`hfModelFitsDevice` judged safetensors rows with the GGUF rule: 0.4
bytes per parameter (the smallest GGUF quant), plus half of system RAM
as offload room. A safetensors chat load goes through transformers,
4-bit by default, and `raise_if_offloaded` rejects any CPU offload. The
badge already uses the 4-bit estimate (`estimateLoadingVram` +
`checkVramFit`), so the filter and the badge disagreed.

## Fix

On a discrete GPU, a safetensors row now gets the badge's verdict
against VRAM only, and is kept unless it is "exceeds". GGUF, MLX, Images
/ Video, catalog-sized rows, and Macs / APUs (`hostPooledMemory`) keep
the existing rule. Downloaded models still always show.

The estimate is still a heuristic. This makes the filter agree with the
badge; it does not prove a kept model will load. I did not run a load.

## Verification

- Live A/B on the Hub page, as in the table.
- New case in `tests/fit-on-device-setting.test.ts`: fails on main,
passes here. The rest of `npm test` fails the same pre-existing tests as

Studio: keep the tool results of the turn in progress when compaction resets mid-turn (#13951)

## Problem

When a chat overflows during a tool loop, checkpoint compaction (the
default `UNSLOTH_CONTEXT_POLICY=checkpoint`) evicts the tool results of
the turn that is still running. Only the newest tool exchange survives.
A model that ran `cat main.py` and then one more command loses the file
it just read, so it reads it again, asks the user for it, or answers
from nothing.

This matches a [Reddit report on
r/unsloth](https://www.reddit.com/r/unsloth/comments/1x3vg5x/i_need_model_recommendatins_for_my_potato_system/)
from a user running gemma-4-E2B with Tools on a 4 GB GPU: the model used
`cat`, edited a script, then forgot it had done so.

## Root cause

Phase two of `fit_checkpoint_context` starts a new epoch with
`truncate_oldest_messages(messages, 0.0)`, which evicts every
unprotected group. `group_turns` puts each assistant `tool_calls`
message and its results in its own group, and the primitive protects
only system and developer turns, the newest user group, the final group,
and explicit pins. The tool exchanges between the newest user message
and the final group are therefore evicted with the old history, even
when they fit. The rolling policy is not affected: it evicts oldest
first and only reaches the current turn after all older history is gone.

## Fix

The reset now also protects the turn in progress (`_live_turn_groups`:
the groups after the newest user message, minus the final group the
primitive already keeps). If the reset does not fit with all of them,
they are released oldest first until it fits. This costs one extra exact
token count per released exchange, only on the request that starts a new
epoch.

Behavior that stays the same:

- Older history is still reset in one step; the carried-forward block,
archive write and forced recall are unchanged.
- The persisted boundary is unchanged: `_branch_boundary` already counts
only messages before the newest user turn.
- A request with no tool exchanges after its newest user message,
including every first fit of a request and `/compact`, takes the same
path as before.
- When only the newest exchange fits, the result and the fallback after
it are the same as before.

Not addressed: the terminal tool's own output cap and repeated reads in
longer tool loops, where answer quality showed no difference either way.

## Verification

`test_a_reset_inside_a_tool_loop_keeps_the_turn_in_progress` covers
everything fitting, releasing only the oldest exchange, and only the
newest fitting. The first two fail on main; the third pins the fallback.
The compaction, recall, archive, overflow and prefix-boundary suites
pass (665 passed; 641 passed, 201 skipped).

Live A/B in Studio with a saved thread, the terminal tool and an
8192-token context. After 11 older exchanges, the model runs two
commands and is asked about the first output without running anything
else. That output ends in a sha256-derived value that appears nowhere in
the prompt; the second output triggers the reset. In every trial
reported here, main dropped 24 messages and this change 22, keeping the
first command's call and result.

| Model | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Q4_K_M | 0/8, a different made-up hash
every trial | 8/8 |
| gemma-4-E2B-it Q4_K_M | 0/7 resets; 1 re-ran the first command | 4/7
resets |

A repeat with a random UUID per trial gave Qwen 0/5 vs 5/5 and gemma 0/4
vs 3/3. Answers are wording-sensitive: asked for the "last line printed
by the first command", Qwen with the change quoted the last line of the
`seq` part of the chain (0/8), while main still invented a hash.

Limitation: when the question names the value ("tell me the value of
SECRET_TOKEN"), main already answers 8/8 because the forced recall finds
the evicted chunk by similarity. Keeping the current turn's output
removes the dependence on that retrieval.

Sync full finetune weights into colocated vLLM in a few load_weights calls (#13901)

When GRPO runs a full finetune with TRL's colocated vLLM engine
(`use_vllm=True`, `vllm_mode="colocate"`), TRL's
`VLLMGeneration.sync_weights` calls the vLLM model's `load_weights` once
per parameter. Every call builds vLLM's weight loader and parameter
lookup again. On Qwen2.5-0.5B that is 290 calls and about 120 to 160 ms
per training step spent in Python overhead. No extra memory is involved,
since the parameters are passed by reference.

This patch replaces that loop, inside Unsloth's existing `sync_weights`
source patch, with grouped calls. The same `(name, tensor)` references
go to vLLM in lists capped at `UNSLOTH_VLLM_WEIGHT_SYNC_BUCKET_MB`
(default 1024), which is one call for small models. Nothing is copied
and every weight loader sees the same tensor, so the vLLM weights after
a sync are bit-identical to the per-tensor path.

The per-tensor loop is kept when:

- `UNSLOTH_VLLM_WEIGHT_SYNC_BUCKET_MB=0`;
- DeepSpeed or FSDP is active, because gathered tensors are only valid
for one iterator step;
- the model is a PEFT model, because TRL unmerges the adapter in place
once iteration ends;
- the TRL source has a different layout (before 1.10), in which case
nothing is patched.

Results on Qwen2.5-0.5B full finetune, 4 GRPO steps, vLLM 0.29, TRL
1.15, exclusive GPU:

| | load_weights calls per sync | sync ms (median, two runs) | vLLM
weights sha256 | step losses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 290 | 159 / 216 | 14ba8627 | reference |
| this PR | 1 | 21 / 24 | 14ba8627 | identical |

In a standalone microbenchmark the vLLM state dict after a one-call sync
is bitwise equal to the per-tensor sync (121 ms vs 8.7 ms), with no
extra peak memory.

New CPU tests in
`tests/version_compat/test_trl_vllm_colocate_weight_sync.py` cover:

- the one-call default;
- the size cap;
- the kill switch;
- the DeepSpeed, FSDP and PEFT fallbacks;
- leaving older TRL layouts untouched.

Studio: rank Latest Unsloth Models by trending weighed against release age (#13969)

## What changed

**Latest Unsloth Models** in the Model hub now ranks uploads by Hugging
Face trending weighed against release age, instead of by repo creation
date alone.

Before, a model that was kept private until launch sorted by the date
its repo was created. Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF went public on
2026-10-15 but its repo was created on 2026-09-19, so it showed up 7th,
below models from weeks ago, while its row said "10h ago" (the row shows
last modified, the list sorted by creation date).

### Ranking

`score = (trendingScore + 2) / (releaseAgeDays + 2) ^ 1.6`, the Hacker
News gravity form:

- The offsets stop a brand new upload with no likes from scoring zero,
and stop a few hours of age from dominating.
- Gravity 1.6 keeps a strong model from this week above a quiet upload
from today, while month-old hits no longer outrank this week's releases
on likes alone.
- **Release age**: the Hub has no publish date. When a repo has at least
5 likes and at least 80% of them are trending (recent), it went public
recently, so its last modification dates it instead of `createdAt`. An
old repo that is only re-touched, with no likes, stays old.

The feed fetches the 100 newest and the 100 most trending Unsloth
uploads, ranks that pool, then continues through the rest by creation
date for scrolling. `fresh` is never sent to the Hub: every listing path
maps it to `createdAt` (`hubListingSort`). The sort menu gains
**Latest** for this ranking; **Newest** stays creation date only.
ModelScope has neither sort, so both fall back to last modified, as
Newest already did.

Order on 2026-10-15: Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B,
NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B,
NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B, LFM2.5-24B-A2B,
Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo, embeddinggemma-2, Qwen3.8-27B.

## Verification

weighting on that day's real Hub numbers, and that `fresh` never reaches

Studio: fix the context meter after tool calls on MLX and transformers (#13913)

After a chat turn where an MLX or transformers model calls a tool
(Python, web search) and then answers, the Context meter in the chat
header adds every earlier pass's output, thinking included, on top of
the final prompt. That output is already inside the final prompt, so it
gets counted twice. On Qwen3-1.7B with Python on, a two-call turn read
7.2k tokens when the conversation held about 4k, and on a Mac the meter
can turn red and show the "generates past the window" advice while the
prompt still fits. The GGUF loop was fixed for this in #12889, but the
MLX and transformers loop still sends the old total.

The tool loop on these models now reports the context the turn leaves
behind: the final pass's prompt plus that pass's own output, the same
figure the GGUF loop sends. The meter already prefers it. The billed
token counts are unchanged, and single-pass replies and the API
passthrough responses look the same as before.

## What changed

composer whenever the system shows classic scroll bars (a mouse
attached, or "Show scroll bars: Always"). The text, headings and list

Context parallel: compose with FSDP2 on a (dp_shard, cp) mesh (#13910)

Stacked on #13848 (Ulysses context parallel, which stacks on #4257).
Depends on #13865 (FSDP2 core), which is merged into this branch; the
change itself is commit 39d648e37.

Context parallelism was DDP only: an FSDP2 launch with
context_parallel_size > 1 was refused. This lets the two compose the way
torchtitan does. The world is laid out as a (dp_shard, cp) mesh, FSDP2
shards parameters over dp_shard x cp flattened (accelerate's
dp_shard_cp), and the sequence split plus the ring or Ulysses
collectives stay on the cp submesh. CP peers hold different tokens of
the same rows, so their gradients are reduced together with the data
parallel ones, and the existing token count normalisation (pre-shard
count divided by the CP size, loss scaled by the world size) stays exact
because FSDP2 averages over the same D x N ranks DDP did.

Usage is unchanged: SFTConfig(context_parallel_size = N) under an FSDP2
launch (UNSLOTH_FSDP2=1 torchrun ..., or an accelerate FSDP2 config);
dp_shard is world size / N.

accelerate's own ParallelismConfig(cp_size = N) is still refused. With
cp_size > 1 accelerate attaches torch's context_parallel SDPA hooks in
prepare(), transformers wraps each step in maybe_context_parallel and
divides num_items_in_batch by the CP size, all of which Unsloth already
does itself. Instead Unsloth installs a ParallelismConfig with
dp_shard_size = D x N and cp_size = 1 next to its own mesh, so
fsdp2_prepare_model shards over mesh["dp_shard_cp"] and the data loader
gives CP peers the same batch (both read the same way since accelerate
1.10, the CP minimum).

FSDP1, DeepSpeed and a ParallelismConfig with dp_replicate, tp or sp
above 1 are refused on every rank before any collective.

Tests
- tests/test_context_parallel.py: FSDP2 accepted, mesh and config
installed and restored by a later trainer, FSDP1 and extra dimensions
refused.
- tests/test_context_parallel_fsdp2_gloo.py: four gloo ranks on CPU,
(dp_shard 2, cp 2). Mesh layout, accelerate's real data loader and
fsdp2_prepare_model, and one patched training step through FSDP2
matching an unsharded model's gradients.
- GPU accuracy on a tiny Llama with LoRA (3 steps, first-step
gradients): (dp_shard, cp) = (1, 2) ring and Ulysses, fp32 and bf16,
gradient accumulation 2, (2, 1) and (2, 2) ring and Ulysses on four GPUs
all match the single GPU run (loss rel err <= 2.5e-5, min grad cosine >=
0.99988). Removing the count division moves loss and gradients by
exactly 0.5, so the check can fail.

Not covered: HSDP or TP with CP, packing / FA3 / FA4 / 4-bit bases under
FSDP2 + CP, multi-node, timing.

Fix optimizer state offload crash with Q-GaLore weight quantization (#13979)

## Summary
With `UNSLOTH_OFFLOAD_OPTIMIZER_STATE=1` and more than one chunk,
Q-GaLore with `weight_quant=True` crashed on the first step:

```
RuntimeError: attempting to assign a gradient of size '[256, 256]' to a tensor of size '[1]'
```

The chunked step hides gradients between chunks and restores them
afterwards, but Q-GaLore weight quantization swaps `p.data` for a one
element placeholder inside `step`, so the original gradient can no
longer be assigned back.

## Change
- `_chunk_safe` now returns False when any param group sets
`weight_quant`. Such optimizers use the existing unchunked route: state
is restored, one normal step runs, and state is offloaded again.
Offloading between steps still applies.
- Nothing changes when the env var is unset, and other optimizers are
unaffected.

## Tests
- `test_weight_quant_q_galore_steps_unchunked` (CPU) checks the gate.
- `test_q_galore_multi_chunk_offload[False|True]` (CUDA, bitsandbytes)
runs the real `QGaLoreAdamW8bit` with a 256 KiB chunk budget for two
steps and checks INT8 weights, scales and gradients match a run without
offload bitwise, with state left on CPU. It failed with the error above
before the change.
- `tests/test_optimizer_state_offload.py`,
`tests/test_formatter_fixed_point.py`,
`tests/test_source_read_encoding.py`: 64 passed, 2 skipped on GPU.

Studio: honour MIG masks and size MIG cards by their slice (#13927)

## Problem

Studio mishandled NVIDIA MIG in three places:

- **MIG UUID mask:** `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=MIG-<uuid>` (or the old
`MIG-GPU-<uuid>/gi/ci` form) was treated as "no mask" by llama.cpp's GPU
sizing. `_get_gpu_memory` then sized the load against whole 40 / 80 GB
cards, and the pin rewrote the child's mask to `"0"`. The child could
land on a different slice or the whole parent card.
- **GPU count:** the physical GPU count included MIG child rows. On one
A100 with two slices the picker offered three GPUs and could write
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2`, which leaves the worker with no device.
- **Numeric mask on a MIG card:** auto-select and llama.cpp were told
the whole card's free memory, not the slice's.

## Fix

- **llama.cpp sizing:** a `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` value that does not map
to nvidia-smi rows (MIG UUIDs, mixed `GPU-a,MIG-b`, an unknown UUID) no
longer reads the whole-card rows. The existing NVML branch already
understands MIG; it reports the slice's memory and hands the child the
MIG UUID.
- **Child mask (`_pinned_child_visibility`):** when the mask cannot be
mapped, the child keeps the user's original mask instead of a widened
`"0"`. ROCm and numeric masks pin as before.
- **MIG card with a numeric mask:** llama.cpp takes the NVML branch, so
the card counts as the slice CUDA exposes. Auto-select ranks it by the
slice's NVML reading, and treats it as unknown when there is no reading.
- **`nvidia.get_mig_gpu_indices()`:** reads the MIG rows of the cached
`nvidia-smi -L`.
- **Physical GPU count:** uses only the `GPU N:` rows. The first
nvidia-smi answer replaces a count that came from the torch fallback,
since torch counts each R570+ MIG slice as a device; after that the
count only grows.
- **One slice per MIG card:** each MIG card is one row backed by a
single visible slice, and the child is pinned to that slice's UUID. It
is the first slice the mask names, otherwise the slice with the least
free memory, so the budget never exceeds the device the child gets. This
holds for llama.cpp, diffusion and training alike. On R570+ drivers,
where one process can see several GPU instances of a card, Studio uses
one of them: conservative, never over budget, and still far closer than
the whole-card size used before.
- **Multi-slice MIG mask:** when torch enumerated every inherited `MIG-`
entry, the child is pinned to the entries behind the picked torch
ordinals instead of the whole mask, and torch ordinals are never mapped
through cached NVML rows.
- **Numeric-prefix masks** (`1gpu2`, `0,1,abc`) keep their cards, read
the way CUDA reads them; a repeated index (`1,1`, `1gpu,1gpu`) gives no
rows, as CUDA itself rejects it. When the slice reading fails, whole
cards keep their nvidia-smi rows; a MIG-only host with no reading at all
falls back to the nvidia-smi rows, so the list is never empty.

Hosts without MIG take exactly the same paths as before.

## Tests

- **New `tests/test_mig_gpu_masks.py`:** covers an A100 with 2x 3g.20gb,
three A100s with card 0 split 3x 2g.10gb, mixed MIG and non-MIG cards,
new and old MIG UUID forms, a UUID prefix, a numeric mask, no NVML and
no MIG.
- **Base vs head:** the behavioural tests fail on main and pass here,
plus guards for the new helpers. Also covers R570-style multi-slice rows
(one slice per card, least free when none is named), repeated indices,
torch ordinals beside cached rows, numeric-prefix masks and a missing
slice reading.
- **Updated existing tests:**
- One existing assertion expected whole-card rows for an unresolvable
UUID mask, which was the bug. It now expects no rows.
  - Two count stubs accept `gpu_rows_only`.
- **57 related test files:** the same failures on main and here, all
pre-existing environment failures.

No MIG-partitioned card was available, so this is proven with spoofed
`nvidia-smi` and NVML output.

GRPO: opt-in zero-variance group exclusion and prompt-level loss aggregation (#13891)

Needs unslothai/unsloth-zoo#1790 (the loss side); with an older
unsloth_zoo the options raise a clear error.

Two ScaleRL options for GRPO, both off by default.

`UNSLOTH_GRPO_ZERO_VARIANCE_EXCLUDE=1` drops groups whose rewards are
all equal from the loss and from its token count. Such groups have zero
advantage, so they only dilute the token mean, and with a KL penalty
they still pull towards the reference.

`UNSLOTH_GRPO_LOSS_AGGREGATION=prompt` averages the token losses within
each group first and then over groups.

Groups only exist during generation, because the loss sees shuffled
micro-batches. So the weights are computed inside
`_generate_and_score_completions`, right after TRL logs
`frac_reward_zero_std`, using TRL's zero-std test on the weighted
rewards and the completion token counts gathered across processes. They
travel with the batch as `unsloth_sample_weight` and replace the loss
type normaliser in unsloth_zoo's GRPO loss.

Exclusion on its own applies to the token-normalised losses (bnpo, dapo,
cispo, vespo). Prompt level applies to every loss type except luspo.
Eval batches are unchanged. The share of excluded groups is logged as
`frac_reward_zero_std_excluded`.

Tests run the shipped helper on synthetic groups, including all-equal
rewards, a reward function that never applies and an unscorable
completion, through TRL's shuffle and split and unsloth_zoo's loss over
one to four simulated processes. Loss and gradients equal the ScaleRL
formulas, and without degenerate groups the result is plain dapo. On a
tiny model with half the groups degenerate, the gradient norm scales by
exactly the predicted 1 / (1 - excluded fraction), and with the options
unset the run is bitwise identical to main.

Not covered: a real multi-process job, prompt-level aggregation with
unequal completion lengths end to end (the tiny model fills the max
length), TRL 0.22.2 and torch 2.6.

Fused Qwen3 q_norm / k_norm RMSNorm + RoPE Triton kernel (opt-in) (#13890)

Qwen3 applies RMSNorm to every query and key head before RoPE. Unsloth
runs this as two `fast_rms_layernorm` calls plus the Triton RoPE kernel.
With the clones around the in-place RoPE, that is 4 forward and about 6
backward launches per layer, plus 3 to 4 autograd Functions. On small
models, where LoRA training is dispatch bound, this region costs about 1
ms of host time per layer per forward and backward.

This PR adds `unsloth/kernels/qk_norm_rope.py`, which does the per-head
RMSNorm and the rotation for Q and K together in one forward launch and
one backward launch:

- Same rounding steps as the current path: fp32 rstd, normed in the
weight dtype, norm output in the activation dtype, rotation in the cos
dtype. bf16 forward outputs are bit-identical to main on the tested
shapes. Backward and fp16/fp32 forward match within rounding.
- Saves the same tensors as today (X, weight, rstd, cos, sin,
positions), so activation memory is unchanged.
- Always writes fresh outputs and never modifies its inputs or the
incoming gradient.
- Supports plain and packed (restarting) position ids, GQA, and head_dim
16 to 1024 (powers of two).
- Eager uses an autograd Function. Compiled graphs use
`torch.library.triton_op` with registered autograd, with no graph
breaks.
- Trainable q_norm/k_norm weights (full fine-tuning) and any shape it
does not cover fall back to the existing path.

The kernel is used by `Qwen3Attention_fast_forward` only when
`UNSLOTH_FUSED_QKNORM_ROPE=1`. With the variable unset, the attention
forward runs the same calls as before, and training is bit-identical to
main.

Testing:
- `tests/test_qk_norm_rope.py`: accuracy against the unfused path and an
fp64 reference across dtypes, head dims 64/128/256, GQA, partial head
blocks and packed positions; compile with fullgraph and the same bytes
as eager; inputs and gradients untouched; trainable-weight fallback.
- Kernel oracle against the Hugging Face Qwen3 norm and rotary code
compiled by Inductor and an fp64 reference: 72 of 72 rows within
tolerance. Errors are equal to or lower than the current path. A 2^-7
perturbation fails every row.
- Deterministic QLoRA training, 20 steps: bit-identical to main with the
variable unset. With it set, the loss difference is the size of the
current path's own compiled-vs-eager rounding, and well below an
eps-perturbed control.
- B200, bf16 LoRA, same-process interleaved timing: about 7 to 10%
faster per step on a 0.6B-shaped model and 3 to 4% on Qwen3-8B layer
shapes. Kernel device time drops 2.9% and 0.7% respectively, with 11
fewer launches per layer per step.

It is opt-in for now because the timings come from a single busy host.
Older torch / Triton versions, T4, and ROCm have not been tried. Once
those are confirmed, it can become the default, with
`UNSLOTH_FUSED_QKNORM_ROPE=0` as the kill switch.

Add optim = "adamw_flash" (FlashAdamW from flashoptim) for lower optimizer memory (#13881)

Setting optim = "adamw_flash" in SFTConfig, GRPOConfig, any other
Unsloth generated config, or UnslothTrainingArguments now selects
FlashAdamW from databricks/flashoptim (Apache-2.0). flashoptim is an
optional dependency, and Unsloth prints an install hint if it is
missing.

By default, bf16 weights keep a 16 bit error correction term in the
optimizer state. The effective master weight is therefore fp32 without a
separate fp32 copy, and the Adam moments stay in the parameter dtype.
That is about 10 bytes per parameter including bf16 gradients, against
16 or more for bf16 weights with an fp32 master and fp32 moments.

On a Qwen2.5-0.5B full fine-tune (150 steps, lr 2e-5) the default
matched fp32 master AdamW: the mean loss over the last 10 steps was
identical (1.5146) and the largest per-step difference was 0.005. torch
peak memory dropped from 10.2 GB to 5.5 GB.

optim_args = "quantize=True" stores the moments in 8 bits for about 8
bytes per parameter, or about 7 with master_weight_bits=24, which is
flashoptim's own default. In the same run that setting ended 0.018
higher in loss, outside the 0.0024 spread between two AdamW seeds, so it
is opt-in. LoRA adapters are fp32 and get no correction term; for them
only quantize=True saves memory.

transformers does not know this optimizer name. The config therefore
stores adamw_torch plus a marker in optim_args that survives
dataclasses.replace and that transformers' own parser accepts.
Trainer.get_optimizer_cls_and_kwargs is wrapped only once someone
selects the optimizer, and every other optim value runs exactly as
before.

These all work with it:
- the weight decay split, LoRA+ groups and embedding learning rate
groups
- betas, eps, schedulers, gradient clipping and gradient accumulation
- checkpoint resume: resuming from step 100 matched the continuous run
to 3e-4 per step on a tiny model

optim_args accepts master_weight_bits, quantize, compress_state_dict,
check_numerics and decouple_lr.



Not covered: real-model convergence beyond 150 steps, FSDP2 / DDP, fp16
training, transformers 4.57.6 / TRL 0.22.2, and GRPO / DPO end to end
(the generated configs were only checked by their code). Exported
weights are bf16: the extra precision lives in the optimizer checkpoint.

Keep the plain capability cache on single-GPU hosts (#13962)

## Problem

#13923 replaced `functools.cache(torch.cuda.get_device_capability)` with
a per-device wrapper, so a no-argument call follows
`torch.cuda.set_device`. On a host with one visible GPU that correctness
gain cannot apply, but every cache hit now runs Python code (resolve the
device, then a dict lookup) instead of the C-level `functools.cache`
hit. The attention helpers call `get_device_capability(Q.device)` on
every eager forward, so single-GPU runs pay a small cost for nothing.

Measured on the cache itself (CPU, 300k calls, best of 7):

| call | main before #13923 | after #13923 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `get_device_capability(Q.device)` | 0.073 us | 0.502 us | 0.096 us |

The last column is the same `functools.cache` object as before #13923;
the residual difference is timer noise.

## Fix

`_cache_device_capability` returns the plain `functools.cache` wrapper
when `torch.cuda.device_count() <= 1`, exactly what main had before
#13923. With one visible device every spelling (no argument, `0`,
`"cuda:0"`, `torch.device("cuda")`, `x.device`) names the same card, so
caching the call is exact. The per-device wrapper is kept for hosts with
two or more visible devices, where it is needed.

## Tests

- New `test_capability_cache_single_device_keeps_the_plain_cache`: a
one-device host gets a `functools.cache` object, probed once per
distinct argument, and re-wrapping does not stack.
- `tests/test_mixed_nvidia_capabilities.py`: 36 passed (the multi-device
cases still use the per-device wrapper).
- On one B200, `test_capability_cache_traces_in_fullgraph` (no argument,
`0`, `"cuda:0"`, `torch.device("cuda")`, `x.device` under
`fullgraph=True`): 5 passed.
- Related suites (bnb NF4 override, compile, context parallel, CE
eviction hints, pre-Volta fast inference, int4, fp8): 209 passed,
unchanged.

Installers (AMD, Linux): a Strix APU defers torch to a discrete card, and a lone gfx1153 warns instead of getting kernel-less wheels (#13931)

## Problem

Two Linux AMD torch routing gaps (#11815, #9932):

- **Strix APU beside a discrete card:** when a Strix APU (gfx1150 /
gfx1151 / gfx1152) was listed first, torch was installed from that APU's
per-arch index. Those wheels carry no other arch.
- With a gfx1151 and an RX 7900 (gfx1100), or an RX 9070 (gfx1201), the
discrete card got no torch kernels.
- This contradicts the installer's own rule for integrated GPUs listed
first (#7776), which installs for the discrete card. Strix was left out
of that rule because it is also the right llama.cpp target when it is
alone.
- **gfx1153 alone:** on Linux it was in no table, so it silently got the
generic ROCm wheel. That wheel has no gfx1153 kernels; AMD publishes
gfx1153 only as an opt-in device pack on its multi-arch index. The "no
wheels for this GPU" warning never showed.

## Fix

- **Strix:**
- `_amd_prefer_discrete_gfx` takes a `torch` mode. For the torch
install, a Strix pick defers to the first discrete card that has a wheel
route, skipping integrated GPUs and gfx906. `_runtime_gfx_target` in
`install_python_stack.py` applies the same rule.
- A warning names the card torch is installed for and how to target the
APU instead (`HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` or `UNSLOTH_ROCM_GFX_ARCH`). The
install summary uses the same pick.
- The deferral needs a readable ROCm version (otherwise there is no
generic tag for the discrete card, so the Strix index is kept, as
before) and no `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION` (an override spoofs every
agent, so the discrete card's wheels would never load).
- When the runtime is not visible yet, the inferred install also uses
the deferred card, and the Radeon repo flag set by the APU's name is
cleared on the handoff.
- **Unchanged:** a lone Strix, any HIP/CUDA/ROCR mask,
`UNSLOTH_ROCM_GFX_ARCH`, Strix + gfx906, Strix + an RDNA 1 card, and
llama.cpp's target.
- **gfx1153:**
- Joins RDNA 1 and Polaris in the "no Linux wheels" list (`install.sh`,
`studio/setup.sh`, `install_python_stack.py`). A lone gfx1153 gets CPU
torch with the explicit warning, plus the opt-in
`UNSLOTH_TORCH_EXTRA=device-gfx1153` hint for AMD's multi-arch index, as
RDNA 1 already has.
- An `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION` to a covered arch still gets ROCm torch.
gfx1153 beside a covered card still installs for that card.
- With no rocminfo or amd-smi, both installers recognise Krackan Point 2
names (Radeon 820M, Ryzen AI 5 330) before the broader gfx1152 patterns,
so a lone gfx1153 is not treated as gfx1152. A Krackan Point 2 CPU or
lspci line is only a fallback: a covered discrete card found by the
lspci scan still wins. The final install summary and `setup.sh`'s
summary keep that inferred gfx1153, and `setup.sh` forwards it to the
llama.cpp installer so the HIP bundle is kept; the guidance no longer
points gfx1153 at Vulkan.
  - llama.cpp's HIP route for gfx1153 is not changed.

Studio's health check on Linux recognises the same Krackan Point 2
names, so a lone gfx1153's CPU torch is not reported as a broken
install.

The KFD-only CPU-index reroute (no rocminfo or amd-smi, readable ROCm
version) is unchanged: there a leading Strix still picks its own index,
as on main, because that single arch export also feeds llama.cpp's
target. Splitting it is a follow-up. Likewise, the "every probed arch is
uncovered" check judges the unmasked inventory, as it already does for
RDNA 1 and Polaris, so a mask that pins gfx1153 beside a covered card
still gets the generic wheel, as on main.

Routing gfx1153 and RDNA 1 to AMD's multi-arch index automatically on
Linux would need the Windows multi-arch handling (device pack detection,
repair, bitsandbytes) ported first. That is left for a follow-up.

## Tests

- **New `tests/studio/install/test_linux_amd_strix_dgpu_gfx1153.py`**,
covering:
  - gfx1151 + gfx1100 and gfx1151 + gfx1201, in both installers;
  - lone gfx1151, masks and the override;
  - lone gfx1153, the HSA override, and gfx1153 beside a covered card;
- Krackan Point 2 cpuinfo and lspci names, an unreadable ROCm version,
an HSA override with a Strix and a discrete card, and the Radeon flag on
the handoff.
- **Base vs head:** the new routing tests fail on main and pass here.
The rest guard the unchanged cases.
- `install.sh` is checked with `bash --posix -n` and `dash -n`, and the
macOS staging leg (bash 3.2) runs it.
- **Full suites:** `tests/studio/install/` (102 files), the `tests/sh`
checks for these helpers and `test_install_resolve_prebuilt.py` all
pass.

FSDP2: first-class LoRA and full finetuning, keep fused LoRA kernels per block (#13865)

FSDP2 through accelerate did not work with Unsloth on current
accelerate. Since accelerate 1.14 the final norm and lm_head get their
own FSDP unit, and Unsloth's forward reads lm_head.weight directly for
the fused cross entropy, so every model with an untied lm_head stopped
at the first step with "aten.mm.default got mixed torch.Tensor and
DTensor". On T4 (float16) the runs that did start skipped their first
steps: accelerate's automatic FSDP2 policy casts the loss to float16
before the GradScaler multiplies it by 65536, which overflows. The fused
LoRA kernels were also switched off for any FSDP.

This PR:

- Detects FSDP2 in every launch mode with the same answer on every rank:
accelerate launch, TrainingArguments(fsdp, fsdp_config version 2), and a
new UNSLOTH_FSDP2=1 for plain torchrun, which exports accelerate's own
FSDP2 launch environment before transformers is imported (per block
wrapping by default, UNSLOTH_FSDP2_RESHARD_AFTER_FORWARD=0 for a ZeRO-2
style run).
- Fills in what accelerate leaves at its defaults: gradients reduced in
float32, no cast of the model outputs, float16 gathers the stored
weights and leaves the casting to autocast like the single GPU run, the
last decoder block stays gathered for backward, and bfloat16 full
finetuning gets float32 master weights (FSDP2 needs one trainable dtype
per unit). A policy the user wrote is never changed.
- Gathers the FSDP units of lm_head and the final norm before the
forward, since Unsloth reads their weights directly.
- Keeps the fused LoRA kernels when every decoder block is its own FSDP
unit (the block's weights are gathered before its forward); FSDP1, a
root-only wrap or a finer wrap still decline them, decided once after
wrapping and agreed across ranks. UNSLOTH_FORCE_FUSED_LORA=1 and
UNSLOTH_FSDP2_FUSED_LORA=0 still work.
- Maps no_sync to set_requires_gradient_sync on accelerate older than
1.11.

Results on Kaggle T4x2 (float16), 1 GPU vs 2 GPU FSDP2, 5 steps: LoRA
loss within 4e-6 and update cosine 0.99997 or better for GA 1 and 2,
Llama (untied) and Qwen2 (tied), in all three launch modes, with the
fused kernels running and never seeing a shard. Full finetuning peak
memory per GPU 3.9 GB vs 8.4 GB for DDP on the same 375M model. Full
finetuning gradients match the single GPU run computed with the exact
cross entropy (cosine 0.999999); the single GPU float16 fused cross
entropy differs from the exact one by itself, which is tracked
separately.

Tests: tests/test_fsdp2_detection.py, tests/test_fsdp2_config.py,
tests/test_fsdp2_wrap_gloo.py (two gloo ranks through accelerate's real
fsdp2_prepare_model, checking that layers which read weights directly
see whole tensors inside per-block units and that a finer wrap declines
them).

Not covered here: save / merge / resume under FSDP2 (follow-up), torch
older than 2.13 on GPU, vision / MoE / Gemma models, multi-node, CPU
offload, timing. 2-GPU packing differs from 1 GPU by the same amount
under DDP and FSDP2 (pre-existing).

Add opt-in optimizer state CPU offload (UNSLOTH_OFFLOAD_OPTIMIZER_STATE=1) (#13882)

Full fine-tuning and large-rank LoRA keep the whole optimizer state on
the GPU through forward, backward and update. This adds an opt-in mode
that keeps the state in pinned host memory between steps and brings it
to the GPU only for the update. It does this one chunk at a time, sized
by UNSLOTH_OFFLOAD_OPTIMIZER_STATE_CHUNK_MB (default 1024). Weights and
gradients stay on the GPU. The design follows prime-rl's state-only
offload, with chunked updates added.

It works through torch optimizer step hooks. Torch AdamW (default,
foreach, fused) and bitsandbytes 8-bit optimizers therefore work
unchanged with accelerate, GradScaler, gradient accumulation, grad
clipping and LR schedulers. Checkpoints save the host copies, and a
resumed run moves the loaded state back to the host right away. Paged
bitsandbytes optimizers and DeepSpeed are left alone. With the variable
unset, nothing is imported or wrapped.

On a T4 (fp16), full fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B at batch size 4:
- Peak allocated memory goes from 9443 to 5347 MiB with adamw_torch, and
from 6685 to 4953 MiB with adamw_8bit.
- Step time rises from about 0.60 s to 1.25 s and from 0.52 s to 0.82 s;
that is the cost of the PCIe copies.
- Losses match the run without offload exactly at every step, including
after resuming from a checkpoint.

A new test covers the opt-in wiring on CPU. On GPU it checks exact step
and checkpoint parity for four optimizer kinds, and a memory bound for
the chunked step.

Not covered: FSDP2 / DDP / multi-GPU, GRPO and DPO end to end (SFT
only), transformers 4.57.6 / TRL 0.22.2 / torch 2.6, and the Kaggle T4
run (these numbers are from Colab T4 and L4).

DPO, ORPO, CPO: opt-in fused preference loss (UNSLOTH_FUSED_PREFERENCE_LOSS=1) (#13870)

Needs unslothai/unsloth-zoo#1782 (the chunked kernel).

With `UNSLOTH_FUSED_PREFERENCE_LOSS=1`, the generated DPO (TRL 0.22 to
0.28), ORPO and CPO trainers score completions from the model's final
hidden states through the new unsloth_zoo chunked kernel, instead of
materialising full logits for the policy and reference passes.

What is reproduced from TRL's concatenated_forward:
- Truncation, padding-free, logits_to_keep, ipo normalisation, ld_alpha,
the RPO and SFT NLL, WPO weights and the logits metrics.
- The loss itself, every loss_type and all logged metrics remain TRL's
own code.

Fallbacks: any input the reimplementation does not cover returns None
and TRL's original forward runs:
- vision batches, encoder-decoder, MoE aux loss
- a LoRA, quantized or sharded output head, or unknown logit transforms

With the flag unset, the generated trainer files are byte-identical to
before.

Results:
- On a T4 in fp16 with Qwen2.5-0.5B LoRA at 8192 tokens per step, peak
allocated memory goes from 10.9 GB to 1.35 GB for DPO and from 12.6 GB
to 1.7 GB for ORPO (identical across three repeats).
- At a fixed bf16 model state the DPO loss error against a float64
oracle drops from 2.3e-3 to 6e-7.
- Tests run TRL's own get_batch_loss_metrics with both forwards on a
float64 model and match loss, metrics and gradients to 1e-9 across 25
DPO and 10 ORPO/CPO configurations. They cover TRL 0.22.2 and 0.24 to
0.28, plus ORPO/CPO on 1.15.

TRL 1.15 already fuses the DPO head upstream, and 0.29 to 1.14 DPO has
no concatenated_forward, so the flag does not touch DPO on those
versions.

Training curves: step 1 is identical (exactly log 2), after that DPO
losses depart from the unfused run because the fused path no longer
rounds logits to bf16 and Adam's early steps amplify small gradient
differences (unfused repeats already differ by up to 0.016 on a T4).
There is no long-run final-quality comparison yet, which is one reason
this is opt-in.

Not covered: DDP / multi-GPU, softcap and logit-scaling models on GPU
(CPU tests only), torch below 2.8 (falls back to half-precision logits

Fix RMSNorm and LayerNorm backward overwriting the incoming gradient (#13888)

The non-Gemma `Fast_RMS_Layernorm.backward` and
`Fast_Layernorm.backward` write dX into the incoming gradient tensor.
PyTorch requires backward never to modify its gradient arguments in
place, and here it breaks results whenever another node or the caller
still reads that tensor:
- Autograd hands the same tensor to both inputs of an add, so in
`norm(x) + x` or `norm1(a) + norm2(b)` the other branch reads dX instead
of dY.
- `y.backward(g)` and `torch.autograd.grad(y, x, g)` overwrite the
caller's `g`.

Against an fp64 reference, the input gradient error on main in these
graphs is 1.2 to 2.6 for fp32, fp16 and bf16.

The decoder path never hit this, because there the norm output feeds a
LoRA or linear backward that returns a fresh tensor.

The fix writes dX into a freshly allocated buffer, as the Gemma path
already does:
- The RMSNorm row and multirow kernels always store into their dX
pointer.
- The LayerNorm kernels gain a dX output pointer.
- The compiled RMSNorm op no longer needs to copy dY first for
non-Gemma.

Results:
- Accuracy: in the shared-gradient graphs the gradient now matches fp64
as closely as eager PyTorch at the same dtype, and the incoming gradient
is left unchanged. Graphs that were already correct give the same error
as before.
- Memory: on Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B shaped models (4-bit LoRA
r=16, bf16, seq 4096, gradient checkpointing off and "unsloth"), peak
allocated memory for a training step is identical to main, to the byte.
Repeated runs of main show no spread. The extra buffer is one
hidden-state-sized tensor that is freed before the step's peak.

Tests: `tests/test_norm_backward_grad_alias.py` checks fp32, fp16 and
bf16 RMSNorm (Gemma and non-Gemma) and LayerNorm against fp64 on graphs
with a shared or caller-owned gradient. The non-Gemma RMSNorm and
LayerNorm cases fail on main and pass with this change.

#13868 touches the same backward: the two compose (keep its `X =
X.view(-1, dim)` and this `dX = torch.empty_like(dY)`), and a trial
merge passes both test sets with `UNSLOTH_RMSNORM_SAVE_OUTPUT` at 0 and
1.

Not covered: speed timing, ROCm / XPU / T4 (memory measured on B200).
Nothing in Unsloth calls `Fast_Layernorm` today, so that half is covered
by the unit tests only.

Core: decide bfloat16, compile and TMA options from every visible NVIDIA GPU on mixed hosts (#13923)

## Problem

On a host with NVIDIA GPUs of different generations, several
process-wide decisions were made from device 0 only. Older cards later
in the list were ignored:

- **bfloat16:** `SUPPORTS_BFLOAT16` and `torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()`
read `get_device_capability()` for the current device (`_gpu_init.py`,
`models/_utils.py`). With an RTX 3090 at index 0 and a T4 or V100 at
index 1, a model split with `device_map="auto"` gets bfloat16 on the old
card.
- **torch.compile kill switches:** the pre-Volta switch
(`device_type.py`) and the gfx906 switch read device 0 only. An sm_61
card at index 1 keeps compile on.
- **GRPO compile options:** the persistent TMA matmul and the cutlass
TMA options were enabled when device 0 is sm90+, even if another visible
card is not.
- **Capability cache:** `torch.cuda.get_device_capability` was replaced
process-wide by `functools.cache(...)`. A call with no arguments is
cached once, so after `torch.cuda.set_device(1)` every later no-argument
call, in any library, still returned device 0's answer.

The HIP branch already checks every visible GPU for bfloat16 and the
gfx10 workarounds (#7922). This brings CUDA in line.

## Fix

- **New `cuda_visible_capabilities()` in `device_type.py`:** returns the
capability of every visible CUDA device. It is guarded per device like
`hip_visible_archs()`: an unreadable card is skipped, and only a failed
device count returns `[]`.
- **New `cuda_gate_capabilities()`:** what the process-wide gates judge:
every card that could be read. That always includes the current device
when it is readable, so a gate is never less strict than the rule before
this PR, and a known old card beside an unreadable one still counts.
- **bfloat16:** enabled only when every visible card is sm80+. On a
mixed host one line says which GPUs turn it off and how to keep
bfloat16: hide them with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`.
- **Compile kill switches:** the pre-Volta switch uses the lowest
visible major, and any visible gfx906 disables compile. The gfx906
switch now also sets the live Dynamo config, like the pre-Volta one, so
regions compiled while unsloth_zoo imported are turned off too.
- **GRPO TMA options:** require every visible card to be sm90+.
- **Capability cache:** keyed per resolved device index. No argument
means the current device. An int, `"cuda:N"`, `"cuda"` or a
`torch.device` resolve through `torch.device`, which Dynamo traces, so
`get_device_capability(Q.device)` inside a `fullgraph=True` region still
compiles. Non-CUDA or unparsable devices are passed through uncached.
- **Flash Attention 2 probe:** still uses the current device. Mixed
placements keep the existing per-placement handling from #13698.

Homogeneous hosts get exactly the same flags and messages, because
"every visible card" and "device 0" agree there.
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""` and `UNSLOTH_ALLOW_CPU=1` still take the
existing no-device branches.

## Tests

- **New `tests/test_mixed_nvidia_capabilities.py`:**
- spoofed capabilities for sm80x2, sm86+sm75 in both orders, sm90+sm61,
and sm61 alone;
  - both bfloat16 chains, the notice and the pre-Volta switch;
  - gfx906 in either position;
  - `set_device(1)` after a no-argument call;
- device spellings, an unreadable card (the gates still judge every
readable card), and the GRPO options.
- **Base vs head:** 10 cases fail on main and pass here. The rest pass
on both sides, since device 0 is already the weakest card in those
shapes.
- **Related suites** (driverless import, compile options, flex
attention, xformers and fp8 gates, pre-Volta fast inference, ROCm bf16):
unchanged on both sides.
- **On a B200**, `test_capability_cache_traces_in_fullgraph` compiles
the wrapper with `fullgraph=True` for no argument, `0`, `"cuda:0"`,
`torch.device("cuda")` and `x.device`: 5 passed. The previous version of
the wrapper failed 3 of them.

Context parallel: Ulysses for Gated DeltaNet hybrids (Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Next) (#13920)

Stacked on #13848 (Ulysses context parallel backend).

Hybrid models with Gated DeltaNet layers could not use context
parallelism. Their linear attention runs a sequential scan (plus a short
causal conv) over the whole sequence, so a sequence shard cannot run it
alone, and the ring backend has no way to pass the recurrent state
across shards.

This builds on the Ulysses backend. For each Gated DeltaNet layer the
projections run on the local sequence shard. A single all-to-all then
moves q, k, v, beta and the decay input from sequence shards to head
shards. Each rank runs the short conv and the chunked gated delta rule
over the full sequence for its heads, using the matching slice of the
conv weight, A_log and dt_bias. A second all-to-all moves the output
back before the gated norm and the output projection. Because the conv
sees the full sequence, no halo exchange is needed. Packed batches pass
global cu_seqlens / seq_idx from packed_seq_lengths to the conv and the
scan, so documents crossing the shard seam stay isolated. If the bound
kernels cannot take those arguments, packing under CP is refused instead
of silently mixing documents.

The full attention layers of these models are Hugging Face modules.
Under Ulysses they are routed through the existing Ulysses attention
exchange and Unsloth's attention dispatcher (flash varlen for packed
batches) via the ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS entry. Outside an active
Ulysses step the entry passes straight through.

Constraints and refusals, checked on every rank at trainer init:
- linear_num_key_heads and linear_num_value_heads must be divisible by
context_parallel_size;
- the ring backend refuses linear attention layers and points to
context_parallel_backend = "ulysses";
- Mamba-2 and other stateful mixers are refused for now;
- eager attention, a non-default attention scale and attention dropout
are refused under Ulysses.

Testing:
- CPU (gloo, 2 ranks):
- CP=2 vs CP=1 gradient parity on tiny Qwen3.5 and Qwen3-Next hybrids,
plus a negative control that runs the stock shard-local layer and must
fail;
  - gate tests;
  - run on transformers 5.17 and 4.57.6.
- 2 GPUs, tiny random models, fp32 and bf16:
- CP=2 vs CP=1 loss and per-parameter gradients, for unpacked batches
and for a packed row whose document crosses the shard seam (reference:
each document run alone).
- With exact torch kernels in fp32 the largest gradient error is 4e-4
relative (most parameters below 1e-5).
- With the fla kernels all non-decay parameters are within 2.5e-2 in
fp32 and 1.5e-2 in bf16.
  - The shard-local control fails with 15% to 74% gradient errors.

Also, while context parallelism is active, the existing hybrid packing
shim no longer derives boundaries from the local shard. Under CP it used
to compute them from the shard and fail its kernel handshake on some
ranks only. Packed batches that carry only restarting position_ids,
without packed_seq_lengths, are refused under Ulysses.

End to end on 2 GPUs: FastModel + LoRA + SFTTrainer on a tiny Qwen3.5,
with context_parallel_size = 2 and the ulysses backend vs a single GPU,
for 6 steps, unpacked and with packing = True (documents crossing the
shard seam).
- Loss matches within 4e-6 and grad norm within 7e-4.
- Every LoRA gradient at the first step matches within 7e-3.
- A control that leaves the Gated DeltaNet layers on their shard shows
6% to 14% gradient errors.
- Unsloth's compiled Qwen3.5 module still dispatches full attention
through the attention registry, and the Ulysses path is confirmed to run
on every step.

Not covered here: Mamba-2 style hybrids, Qwen3-Next through FastModel,
real weights, and more than 2 GPUs.

Studio installer: cover the GPUs CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES hides when picking the llama.cpp CUDA bundle (#13924)

## Problem

The llama.cpp CUDA bundle was picked from the GPUs
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` leaves visible. Torch routing and `setup.sh` look
at every physical GPU.

On a GTX 1080 + RTX 4090 host installed with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`,
the installer picked a bundle covering sm_89 only. Once the mask is gone
(a new shell, Studio picking the 1080, or a split across both cards),
llama-server fails on the 1080 with "no kernel image is available".

## Fix

- **New `_mask_widened_sms(host)`:** when the mask hides a card whose SM
the visible cards lack, it returns every SM the hardware has. It returns
None when nothing is hidden, or when the physical or visible caps are
unknown (main's unknown-GPU safeguard then decides as before).
- **`linux_cuda_choice_from_release` and
`published_windows_cuda_attempts`:**
- First try a bundle covering every physical card. On Windows only
bundles with SM metadata count, so a legacy bundle of unknown coverage
never passes as a widening.
- The visible-only candidates follow as later fallbacks, so anything
that installed on main still installs if the widened one fails its
checksum or validation. If no bundle covers every card, today's
visible-only choice is used, with a log line saying so.
- The first try does not log the "no published CUDA bundle covers"
warning or the driver-floor message, so a working fallback stays quiet.

- **Install reuse:** on a host where the mask hides such a card, the
install profile also records the physical caps, so an earlier narrow
install is re-selected once. Every other host keeps exactly the profile
it had, so nobody else reinstalls.

Coverage only widens. If no bundle covers the hidden card, the result is
exactly what main picks today. The mask still decides which card runs at
runtime. `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""` / `-1` is unchanged: that path
already swaps in the physical caps.

## Tests

- **New `tests/studio/install/test_llama_cuda_covers_masked_gpus.py`:**
- GTX 1080 + RTX 4090 with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`: Linux and Windows
pick the bundle covering both cards, including through
`_linux_published_attempts`.
- When no bundle covers both, the visible-only choice stands, with no
uncovered warning.
- The visible-only candidates stay as fallbacks on Linux, the
published-attempts path and Windows; unknown coverage and unknown
visible caps do not widen; the profile key changes only on masked mixed
hosts.
- **Base vs head:** the new tests fail on main and pass here.
- **Full installer suite** (`tests/studio/install/` plus
`test_install_resolve_prebuilt.py`, 103 files): all pass.

GRPO: exclude masked rows from clip_ratio metrics for one-token completions (#13883)

The clip ratio metrics in the GRPO compute_loss use a helper that treats
any tensor of width 1 as a sequence level importance ratio and averages
it without the completion mask. When completions are a single token wide
the token level clip indicators are also width 1, so rows that are fully
masked are counted in the denominator and clip_ratio/low_mean,
clip_ratio/high_mean, clip_ratio/region_mean and cispo_clip_ratio come
out too small.

The helper now only takes the plain mean when the indicator is width 1
and the completion mask is wider, which is the real sequence level case.
This matches the fix in unsloth-zoo #1772. The loss is unchanged; only
the logged metrics move, and only for one-token completions.

instead of 0.5 for two clipped tokens out of two unmasked rows) and
passes here.

Opt-in token-balanced and token-budget SFT micro-batches (#13878)

Padding-free and packed SFT batches have a fixed row count but a very
uneven token count. One micro-batch with a few long rows sets peak
memory, and one data-parallel rank with the long rows makes the others
wait at the gradient all-reduce. This adds two opt-in controls. Both are
off by default, and with neither set nothing is installed.

`UNSLOTH_TOKEN_BALANCE=1` reorders the training sampler within each
optimizer step. The step's rows are spread over ranks and gradient
accumulation slots with equal token sums, using a Karmarkar-Karp largest
differencing partition. Each step keeps exactly the same rows, so
`num_items_in_batch` and the loss normalization are unchanged. Rows only
move between ranks when `average_tokens_across_devices` is on; otherwise
each rank keeps its rows and only its accumulation slots are balanced.
The wrap happens after accelerate prepares the dataloader, so seeded
shuffling is preserved. `group_by_length` and `batch_rebalance` are left
alone.

`UNSLOTH_TOKEN_BUDGET=<tokens>` runs a micro-batch larger than the
budget as several forward and backward passes over whole sequences, each
divided by the same `num_items_in_batch`, so the result equals the
unsplit step. Padding-free batches split between sequences, and padded
batches split by rows. Vision batches, DeepSpeed and FSDP are not split.

On a tiny Llama with LoRA, with both controls off the run is bitwise
identical to main. With them on, the per-step token counts are identical
and the loss differs by about 1e-4, at the bf16 noise floor. On that
run, balancing cut the largest micro-batch from 1017 to 613 tokens and
the peak memory from 666 to 467 MiB, and a 200-token budget held peak
memory at 364 MiB. On two GPUs with DDP, the median per-rank token
imbalance went from 40% to 6%. CPU tests cover the partitioner, the step
invariants against accelerate's batch sharding, and exact loss and
gradient equality for split batches. They pass on transformers 4.57.6
with TRL 0.22.2 and on transformers 5.17 with TRL 1.15.

Not covered: no speed claim (tiny model, shared GPUs), real-size models,
TRL `packing=True` on GPU, DeepSpeed / FSDP (split disabled there,
balancing untested), iterable datasets (ignored), torch 2.6. Bucket
padding was not added: torch.compile built one graph across lengths 38
to 1017 on the tiny Llama, so there were no recompiles to remove.

Build RoPE cos/sin caches only on the device that uses them (#13855)

Unsloth's rotary classes (LlamaRotaryEmbedding and its scaled
subclasses, LongRope, Gemma) built their cos/sin cache for every visible
GPU in `__init__` and again on every growth. LlamaModel_fast_forward
also grew the cache to `max_position_embeddings` on its first forward.
Under torchrun, every rank therefore allocated the full table on every
GPU, and opened a CUDA context on each peer. For a 1M-context model that
is 512 MiB of fp16 cos/sin per GPU per rank.

The cache is now built per device the first time that device reads it,
and only with the rows callers ask for. That is the larger of this
batch's length and `max_seq_length`, rounded up to the existing 8192
step, and never below the 32768 rows the cache used to start with.
`current_rope_size` and the cache dtype still change exactly as before,
and each row depends only on its position, so values are bit-identical.
Devices that were built before a growth rebuild lazily on their next
read. `get_cached`, `extend_rope_embedding` and `forward` keep their
signatures. `extend_rope_embedding` gains an optional `materialize_len`.
Gemma2's attention now reads the cache through `get_cached` instead of
indexing the per-device list.

On Kaggle T4x2 (2-rank torchrun, a Llama-shaped model with 1M max
positions, LoRA under DDP, 3 repeats per arm):
- each process's memory on its own GPU drops from 1642 to 458 MiB;
- its memory on the peer GPU drops from 1454 to 142 MiB;
- the loss is identical at every step.

The remaining peer allocation comes from the gradient checkpointing
buffers in unsloth-zoo, not from RoPE (unslothai/unsloth-zoo#1776 makes
those lazy per device). On one GPU, loss, gradient norm and greedy
generation are bitwise identical to main for Llama and Gemma2, and
torch.compile graph breaks are unchanged.

`tests/test_rope_cache_current_device.py` runs the classes on CPU with a
fake 4-device count. It fails on main and passes here.

Context parallel: Ulysses backend with packing and varlen attention (#13848)

Stacked on #4257 (base is its branch; retarget to `main` once it
merges).

Adds a Ulysses backend for context parallelism:
`SFTConfig(context_parallel_size = N, context_parallel_backend =
"ulysses")`. Ring attention (#4257) shards the sequence inside SDPA, so
it cannot run varlen kernels and turns packing / padding-free off.
Ulysses instead exchanges sequence shards for head shards around
attention, so attention sees the whole sequence for `H / N` heads and
the normal dispatcher runs unchanged: packing, padding-free, flash
varlen, torch varlen, SDPA packed segments and xformers all keep
working, and FA4 / FA3 engage wherever they engage without CP (torch's
flash path).

How it works:
- `unsloth/utils/ulysses.py`: an autograd all-to-all (`[B, H, T/N, D] ->
[B, H/N, T, D]` and back for the output; backward is the inverse
exchange, no scaling). When `N > n_kv_heads`, K/V heads are repeated so
every rank gets whole groups; autograd sums the copies' gradients back.
Needs `n_heads % N == 0` and `n_kv_heads` and `N` dividing one another,
checked on every rank at trainer init.
- `run_attention` routes through the exchange when a Ulysses manager is
active, rebuilding `AttentionConfig` / `AttentionContext` for the local
heads and global length, so the existing backends and guards
(`flash_impl_allows`, varlen int32 guard, padded tail segment) apply as
is.
- `ContextParallelManager` (Ulysses): builds `shift_labels` on the full
sequence after masking packed document starts, keeps (or builds
per-document) `position_ids`, pads to a multiple of `N`, and keeps this
rank's contiguous slice. `packed_seq_lengths` stays global, since
attention sees the whole sequence; the CP pad tail becomes its own
segment.
- Ring-only restrictions stay ring-only: SDPA forcing and the varlen
refusal in `select_attention_backend`, the fp32 downcast,
`UNSLOTH_CP_GQA`, the trainer's packing / padding-free / `eval_packing`
block, `sync_each_batch`, and the sm80 requirement.
- Loss is the same contract as #4257: the pre-shard target count summed
over the world, divided by `N` once.

Tests:
- `tests/test_ulysses.py` (CPU, gloo, 2 and 4 ranks): exchange order and
round trip; forward and Q/K/V gradients against full-sequence attention
for MHA, GQA, MQA with 2x and 4x KV replication, fp32 and fp64, odd
lengths padded; packed documents crossing every shard seam; the real
`run_attention` SDPA path for dense and packed rows.
- `tests/test_context_parallel.py`: contiguous sharding after the global
shift, packed lengths kept global with per-document positions and masked
document starts, ring refusing packed batches, routing through the
exchange, head-count and sm80 checks at init.

with no targets). Reference is CP=1 on the same rows; gates are loss
